title: Why is it called a jigsaw puzzle?
description: The first jigsaw puzzles were maps glued to wood and cut apart for geography lessons — and the saw that cut them gave the puzzle its name.

body.heading: A map, a saw, and a lesson
paragraphs: In the 1760s, a London mapmaker named John Spilsbury had a bright idea for teaching geography: paste a map onto a thin board of wood, then cut along the borders so children could rebuild the world piece by piece. These “dissected maps” were the first jigsaw puzzles.

The name arrived with the tool. Later makers cut their boards with a fine saw called a jigsaw (also known as a fretsaw), whose blade dances up and down. The puzzles were not always cut with one — but the name stuck, as names do.

body.heading: From classroom to craze
paragraphs: For over a century puzzles stayed educational and expensive, each one cut from wood by hand. Cardboard and die-cutting changed everything in the early 1900s, and during the Great Depression of the 1930s, cheap weekly jigsaw puzzles became a full-blown craze — a lot of entertainment for very little money.

The pieces evolved too. Early puzzles had no interlocking knobs; the picture simply fell apart if you breathed on it. The satisfying click of a modern piece is a later invention, and puzzlers defend it fiercely.

body.heading: Try it: make a dissected map
paragraphs: Print or draw a simple map — your street, your country, a treasure island of your own invention — glue it to stiff card, and cut along the borders with scissors. You have just remade Spilsbury's original invention.

Then swap puzzles with a friend and time each other. Geography teachers have known for 250 years what you will discover: you learn the shape of a place far better by rebuilding it than by looking at it.

takeaway: Jigsaw puzzles began as geography lessons cut from wood — the saw in the name is a clue to how they were made.
